healthbR, microdatasus and read.dbc: reading DATASUS microdata in R

Source: vignettes/healthbr-vs-microdatasus.Rmd
healthbr-vs-microdatasus.Rmd

Why this vignette

If you read DATASUS microdata in R – deaths from SIM, live births from SINASC, hospital admissions from SIH – there are three routes, and they work at different layers:

  • read.dbc, by Daniela Petruzalek, is a reader: hand it a .dbc file you downloaded and it returns a data frame. For a decade it was what every other tool called underneath.
  • microdatasus, by Raphael Saldanha, described in Saldanha et al. (2019), downloads and labels: fetch_datasus() fetches the files from the Ministry’s FTP and process_*() replaces codes with labels. It is the usual answer to “how do I get DATASUS into R”.
  • healthbR downloads, caches and types, reads SIH and SI-PNI from a Parquet mirror with per-file provenance, and covers systems and surveys outside DATASUS.

This vignette puts the three side by side on the same files: what each one returns, how long it takes, the same tasks written in each, and the mirror’s Parquet read with no package at all. Pick the one that fits your workflow – or combine them.

Two measurement sessions, same Windows laptop, R 4.6.1, a residential connection in Brazil:

  • 2026-10-14 (read.dbc, speed, side-by-side code, Parquet): healthbR 0.4.0.9000 (development version), microdatasus 3.0.0, read.dbc 1.2.0, arrow 25.0.1, duckdb 1.5.5, dplyr 1.2.1.
  • 2026-09-05 (the SIH, SIM and SINASC walk-throughs further down): healthbR 0.3.1 (development version), microdatasus 3.0.0, which is still the CRAN version, arrow 25.0.0, dplyr 1.2.1. Row counts, record sets and column types of the SIH file were measured again on 2026-10-14 and had not changed.

Timings depend on your network; row counts, column types and values do not. Nothing here runs at build time (eval = FALSE): the outputs are pasted from those sessions, and the code is complete so you can rerun it.

Three layers

read.dbc 1.2.0 microdatasus 3.0.0 healthbR
You give it a .dbc path system, years, months, UFs system, years, months, UFs
It downloads – from the DATASUS FTP from the FTP, or from the healthbr-data Parquet mirror (SIH, SI-PNI)
Columns come back as the DBF declares them: numeric fields parsed by foreign all character (fetch_datasus()); labels after process_*() typed by meaning: dates as Date, counts and values numeric, codes kept as character
Keeps a copy – – partitioned Parquet cache; a repeated call does not download
Dependencies foreign 12 packages more (arrow optional, for the mirror and lazy queries)
Writes .dbc yes (dbf2dbc()) – –
On CRAN no: archived on 2025-12-14 yes yes (0.4.0)

read.dbc today

CRAN archived read.dbc on 2025-12-14, “as issues were not corrected in time”; the last release, 1.2.0, is from 2025-11-28. It still works – every number below was measured with it – but it now installs from source:

# from the CRAN archive (needs Rtools on Windows: the package compiles C)
install.packages(
  "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/read.dbc/read.dbc_1.2.0.tar.gz",
  repos = NULL, type = "source"
)
# or the development version
# remotes::install_github("danicat/read.dbc")

The other two no longer depend on it. microdatasus 3.0.0 “removes the dependency on read.dbc and reads DBC files with vendored C code adapted from healthbR” (its NEWS), and exports that reader as microdatasus::read_dbc(). healthbR has shipped its own decompressor from the start: Mark Adler’s blast.c plus a small dbc2dbf.c (see inst/COPYRIGHTS). All three decode the same PKWare DCL stream, and on the same file they decompress at the same speed (next section). If a script of yours calls read.dbc::read.dbc(file) and you would rather not depend on an archived package, microdatasus::read_dbc(file) is the closest drop-in; it returns every column as character.

Speed

Two SIH files from the FTP, competence 2023-01: Roraima, the smallest (349 KB .dbc, 4,734 admissions), and São Paulo, the largest (16.4 MB, 210,225 admissions). Each cold run is a new R process with an empty healthbR cache, so nothing is reused between runs; the figures are the median of three runs, package loading excluded. All five routes returned the same rows, and the same set of N_AIH.

One file, from nothing:

Route RR SP
read.dbc: curl_download() + read.dbc() 0.9 s 9.7 s
microdatasus: fetch_datasus() 2.7 s 18.0 s
healthbR from the FTP: sih_data(source = "datasus") 1.3 s 16.4 s
healthbR from the mirror: sih_data() 7.4 s 7.7 s
No package: arrow::read_parquet(<mirror URL>) 0.4 s 1.1 s

The same file again:

Route RR SP
read.dbc, microdatasus download again download again
healthbR, new R session, cache on disk 2.3 s 3.5 s
healthbR, same R session 0.8 s 2.3–2.8 s

Decompression only, the .dbc already on disk (bench::mark(), five iterations): read.dbc, microdatasus::read_dbc() and healthbR’s internal reader took 40–49 ms on RR and 5.2–5.8 s on SP – the same algorithm, within 10% of each other. Reading the mirror’s Parquet of the same file from disk took 25 ms and 0.73 s.

What the tables say:

  • For one small file the FTP wins. read.dbc is the fastest route from nothing to a data frame on RR; healthbR’s first call to the mirror pays for its manifest (11 MB, one entry per published file with MD5, size and timestamp), which it downloads once and revalidates by ETag afterwards.
  • For a large file the mirror wins. On SP the Parquet is 10 MB against 16 MB of .dbc, and it needs no decompression: healthbR from the mirror (7.7 s) beats every FTP route, including its own (16.4 s, which also writes the cache and types the columns).
  • Repetition is where a cache counts. read.dbc and microdatasus download and decompress again every time; healthbR reads its local Parquet.
  • Typing has a cost, and healthbR pays it at read time. The gap between arrow::read_parquet() (1.1 s on SP) and a warm sih_data() (2.3–2.8 s) is mostly converting dates and numbers and attaching provenance. sih_data(parse = FALSE) skips the conversion.

These measurements found three slow paths in healthbR – date parsing row by row, a needless copy of every cached row, and a lazy query that listed the whole mirror before reading one year – fixed in the version measured here (see NEWS); before the fixes a warm SP read took 7.7 s and the lazy year below 16.7 s.

The same tasks, side by side

Read one month of SIH for one state 

# read.dbc: you build the FTP path and download
f <- tempfile(fileext = ".dbc")
curl::curl_download(
  "ftp://ftp.datasus.gov.br/dissemin/publicos/SIHSUS/200801_/Dados/RDRR2301.dbc", f
)
rr_r <- read.dbc::read.dbc(f, as.is = TRUE)

# microdatasus
rr_m <- microdatasus::fetch_datasus(
  year_start = 2023, month_start = 1, year_end = 2023, month_end = 1,
  uf = "RR", information_system = "SIH-RD"
)

# healthbR
rr_h <- healthbR::sih_data(year = 2023, month = 1, uf = "RR")

The file name encodes the system, file type, state and competence (RD + RR + 23 + 01); read.dbc leaves that and the directory, which changes by system and period, to you. Column types differ:

table(vapply(rr_r, function(x) class(x)[1], ""))   # read.dbc
#> character   integer   numeric
#>        77        17        19
table(vapply(rr_m, function(x) class(x)[1], ""))   # microdatasus
#> character
#>       113
table(vapply(rr_h, function(x) class(x)[1], ""))   # healthbR
#> character      Date   integer   numeric
#>       101         3         7         5

read.dbc parses what the DBF declares numeric: the values and counts, but also some coded fields – MORTE comes back an integer while SEXO stays text – and it leaves dates as text (DT_INTER is "20221213"). healthbR decides by meaning: dates become Date, values and counts numeric, codes stay character (MORTE is "0"/"1"), so they join with sih_dictionary() and do not change type between years.

Deaths per competence for a year 

# read.dbc: twelve downloads, all rows read
deaths_r <- vapply(1:12, function(m) {
  f <- tempfile(fileext = ".dbc")
  curl::curl_download(sprintf(
    "ftp://ftp.datasus.gov.br/dissemin/publicos/SIHSUS/200801_/Dados/RDRR23%02d.dbc", m
  ), f)
  sum(read.dbc::read.dbc(f, as.is = TRUE)$MORTE == 1)
}, numeric(1))

# microdatasus: twelve downloads, all rows in memory, then filter
deaths_m <- microdatasus::fetch_datasus(
  2023, 1, 2023, 12, uf = "RR", information_system = "SIH-RD"
) |>
  dplyr::filter(MORTE == "1") |>
  dplyr::count(MES_CMPT)

# healthbR: lazy query over the mirror, only the matching rows travel
deaths_h <- healthbR::sih_data(year = 2023, uf = "RR", lazy = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::filter(MORTE == "1") |>
  dplyr::count(month) |>
  dplyr::collect()
Route RR 2023, 12 competences
read.dbc loop 10.2 s
microdatasus 12.7 s
healthbR, lazy = TRUE 3.7 s
duckdb over the 12 mirror URLs, no package (next section) 1.4 s

All four return the same 1,450 deaths, month by month (113, 120, 175, 166, 118, 78, 97, 144, 105, 104, 128, 102).

Labels 

# microdatasus: one call
rr_mp <- microdatasus::process_sih(rr_m)

# healthbR: a join with the dictionary, when you want it
rr_h |>
  dplyr::count(MORTE) |>
  dplyr::left_join(healthbR::sih_dictionary("MORTE"), by = c("MORTE" = "code"))

# read.dbc: labels are yours to bring

The mirror without healthbR

The Parquet files healthbR reads are public. The healthbr-data mirror publishes one file per DATASUS file, at a path that follows the FTP’s competence and state, with every column as the original string:

url <- "https://data.sidneybissoli.com/sih/rd/ano=2023/mes=01/uf=RR/part-0.parquet"
rr_a <- arrow::read_parquet(url)
dim(rr_a)
#> [1] 4734  113

# a year in one SQL query, nothing downloaded but the matching bytes
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
DBI::dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs; LOAD httpfs;")
urls <- sprintf(
  "'https://data.sidneybissoli.com/sih/rd/ano=2023/mes=%02d/uf=RR/part-0.parquet'", 1:12
)
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, paste0(
  "SELECT count(*) AS deaths FROM read_parquet([", toString(urls), "]) ",
  "WHERE MORTE = '1'"
))
#>   deaths
#> 1   1450
DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

Which files exist, and what each came from (FTP URL, MD5 and size of the .dbc, record count, Parquet SHA-256), is in https://data.sidneybissoli.com/sih/rd/manifest.json – what healthbR::sih_status() reads. If you know the files you want, this is the fastest route in this vignette (0.4 s for RR, 1.1 s for SP, 1.4 s for the year). What healthbR adds on top: the paths and the manifest handled for you, types, the local cache, year/month/uf_source columns, the provenance attached to the result, years whose schemas differ, and the FTP fallback when the mirror does not answer. The mirror covers SIH-RD (1992–present) and SI-PNI; for SIM, SINASC, SIA, SINAN and CNES all three packages read the FTP.

The same reader, three philosophies

All three read the same bytes. What differs is what happens after.

read.dbc returns the DBF as it is declared. The DBF header types each field; foreign::read.dbf() turns numeric fields into numbers and keeps the rest as text (as.is = TRUE stops it from making factors). Nothing is added or renamed.

healthbR keeps the codes and types the columns. SEXO stays "1"/"3", MORTE stays "0"/"1", DT_INTER becomes a Date, VAL_TOT a double, IDADE an integer. Labels live in sih_dictionary(), sim_dictionary(), sinasc_dictionary(), joined when you want them. The default parse = TRUE converts only genuinely quantitative and date fields; coded categorical fields stay character so they join cleanly with the dictionaries and with other years.

microdatasus separates fetching from processing. fetch_datasus() returns every column as character, exactly as the DBF has it. process_sih(), process_sim(), process_sinasc() then replace the codes with labels (SEXO becomes "Masculino"/"Feminino", MORTE becomes "Não"/"Sim"), convert dates, split the SIM age field into one column per unit and, with municipality_data = TRUE, join municipality names, coordinates and altitude. The result is a tibble of character columns.

None is wrong. Labels are what you want for a table in a report; codes are what you want to join against a dictionary, compare years, or feed a model; the DBF as declared is what you want when you are building your own pipeline. The trap is mixing them: after process_sih(), MORTE == 1 is FALSE on every row, and substr(DT_INTER, 5, 6) is no longer the month, because both were rewritten. Read the outputs below before choosing.

One download, compared: SIH, Roraima, competence 2023-01

Measured on 2026-09-05 (healthbR 0.3.1 dev); dimensions, record sets and types re-measured on 2026-10-14.

Roraima is the smallest SIH file; January 2023 has 4,734 admissions.

library(healthbR)
library(microdatasus)
library(dplyr)

# healthbR ---------------------------------------------------------------
rr_h <- sih_data(year = 2023, month = 1, uf = "RR")
#> ℹ Reading SIH data from R2: 2023/01 (1 UF(s))...

dim(rr_h)
#> [1] 4734  116

# microdatasus -------------------------------------------------------------
rr_m <- fetch_datasus(year_start = 2023, month_start = 1,
                      year_end = 2023, month_end = 1,
                      uf = "RR", information_system = "SIH-RD")
dim(rr_m)
#> [1] 4734  113

rr_mp <- process_sih(rr_m)
dim(rr_mp)
#> [1] 4734  121

# read.dbc -----------------------------------------------------------------
dim(rr_r)    # from the side-by-side section above
#> [1] 4734  113

Same 4,734 rows; the sets of N_AIH are identical in the three. healthbR adds three columns (year, month, uf_source: the competence and state the file belongs to, which the AIH record itself does not carry); process_sih() adds eight (munResStatus, munResTipo, munResNome, munResUf, munResLat, munResLon, munResAlt, munResArea).

The same five records, three ways:

cols <- c("N_AIH", "SEXO", "COD_IDADE", "IDADE", "MORTE", "DT_INTER",
          "DIAG_PRINC", "MUNIC_RES", "VAL_TOT")

as.data.frame(head(rr_h[cols], 5))
#>           N_AIH SEXO COD_IDADE IDADE MORTE   DT_INTER DIAG_PRINC MUNIC_RES  VAL_TOT
#> 1 1423100411392    3         4    18     0 2022-12-13       O809    140017   568.80
#> 2 1423100911661    1         4    83     0 2022-12-26       J189    140010   994.59
#> 3 1423100911672    3         4    65     0 2022-12-03       I219    140010   620.12
#> 4 1423100911683    1         4    58     0 2022-12-26       I248    140020   333.08
#> 5 1423100911694    1         4    35     0 2022-11-01       A499    140010 11202.59

as.data.frame(head(rr_m[cols], 5))
#>           N_AIH SEXO COD_IDADE IDADE MORTE DT_INTER DIAG_PRINC MUNIC_RES  VAL_TOT
#> 1 1423100411392    3         4    18     0 20221213       O809    140017    568.8
#> 2 1423100911661    1         4    83     0 20221226       J189    140010   994.59
#> 3 1423100911672    3         4    65     0 20221203       I219    140010   620.12
#> 4 1423100911683    1         4    58     0 20221226       I248    140020   333.08
#> 5 1423100911694    1         4    35     0 20221101       A499    140010 11202.59

as.data.frame(head(rr_mp[c(cols, "munResNome")], 5))
#>           N_AIH      SEXO COD_IDADE IDADE MORTE   DT_INTER DIAG_PRINC MUNIC_RES  VAL_TOT munResNome
#> 1 1423100411392  Feminino      Anos    18   Não 2022-12-13       O809    140017    568.8      Cantá
#> 2 1423100911661 Masculino      Anos    83   Não 2022-12-26       J189    140010   994.59  Boa Vista
#> 3 1423100911672  Feminino      Anos    65   Não 2022-12-03       I219    140010   620.12  Boa Vista
#> 4 1423100911683 Masculino      Anos    58   Não 2022-12-26       I248    140020   333.08  Caracaraí
#> 5 1423100911694 Masculino      Anos    35   Não 2022-11-01       A499    140010 11202.59  Boa Vista

Note DT_INTER: the admissions billed in competence 2023-01 happened in November and December 2022. In all three routes the file (or year/month, year_start/month_start) selects the billing competence, not the admission date; the admissions of a calendar year keep arriving for a few competences after it (measured on the whole mirror: the four competences after a year close 99.7–99.9% of its admissions). No package can change that; all should be used with it in mind.

And the trap, in one line each:

sum(rr_h$MORTE == 1)          # healthbR: "1"; R compares it as text
#> [1] 113
sum(rr_r$MORTE == 1)          # read.dbc: integer, as the DBF declares it
#> [1] 113
sum(rr_m$MORTE == "1")        # microdatasus, raw: character code
#> [1] 113
sum(rr_mp$MORTE == 1)         # microdatasus, processed: the code is gone
#> [1] 0
table(rr_mp$MORTE)
#>  Não  Sim
#> 4621  113

Same 113 deaths; the last line is the one that silently returns zero in a script written against codes. With healthbR the label is a join away:

sih_dictionary("MORTE")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   variable description              code  label
#>   <chr>    <chr>                    <chr> <chr>
#> 1 MORTE    Óbito durante internação 0     Não
#> 2 MORTE    Óbito durante internação 1     Sim

What comes with the data: provenance

From the mirror, the tibble carries the source it was served from and one row per DATASUS file behind it – URL, MD5 and size of the .dbc, record count, when it was processed and by which pipeline version:

attr(rr_h, "healthbr_source")
#> [1] "r2"

attr(rr_h, "healthbr_provenance") |>
  select(year, month, uf, records, source_hash_md5, source_size_bytes,
         processing_timestamp)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>    year month uf    records source_hash_md5                  source_size_bytes processing_timestamp
#>   <int> <int> <chr>   <dbl> <chr>                                        <dbl> <chr>
#> 1  2023     1 RR       4734 12e74d4b059589ceb47e4136e3b2ce5f            349244 2026-03-09 03:05:34.463049

sih_status() gives the same for every published partition, which is how you find out which competences exist and whether the Ministry re-issued a file (the MD5 changes):

st <- sih_status()
nrow(st)
#> [1] 11157
range(st$year)
#> [1] 1992 2026
st |> filter(uf == "RR", year == 2023, month == 1) |>
  select(records, source_hash_md5, parquet_sha256, pipeline_version)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   records source_hash_md5                  parquet_sha256                                                   pipeline_version
#>     <dbl> <chr>                            <chr>                                                            <chr>
#> 1    4734 12e74d4b059589ceb47e4136e3b2ce5f bab1c2fdda7b09a6117169156f51846e095de0bc502fec9adecf90d2e1f08474 1.0.0

microdatasus 3.0.0 has track_source = TRUE, which appends a source column with the name of the .dbc each row came from; read.dbc knows only the path you gave it. Neither records hashes or timestamps, and the FTP does not offer them. If your derived product needs to say exactly which files it was built from, this is the difference that matters.

SIM: mortality, Acre 2022

Measured on 2026-09-05.

# healthbR
ac_h <- sim_data(year = 2022, uf = "AC")
#> ℹ Downloading SIM data: AC 2022...
dim(ac_h)
#> [1] 4159   90

# microdatasus
ac_m  <- fetch_datasus(year_start = 2022, year_end = 2022, uf = "AC",
                       information_system = "SIM-DO")
ac_mp <- process_sim(ac_m)
dim(ac_m); dim(ac_mp)
#> [1] 4159   87
#> [1] 4159  100

Same 4,159 deaths (1.5 s healthbR, 2.1 s + 0.7 s microdatasus). The interesting column is age. SIM stores it as three characters: the first is the unit (0 minutes, 1 hours, 2 days, 3 months, 4 years, 5 years over 100) and the last two the value. The two packages decode it differently (read.dbc leaves it as the three-character field):

sim_dictionary("IDADE")
#> # A tibble: 6 × 4
#>   variable description                 code  label
#>   <chr>    <chr>                       <chr> <chr>
#> 1 IDADE    Idade (1º dígito = unidade) 0     Minutos (< 1 hora)
#> 2 IDADE    Idade (1º dígito = unidade) 1     Horas
#> 3 IDADE    Idade (1º dígito = unidade) 2     Dias
#> 4 IDADE    Idade (1º dígito = unidade) 3     Meses
#> 5 IDADE    Idade (1º dígito = unidade) 4     Anos (0-99)
#> 6 IDADE    Idade (1º dígito = unidade) 5     Anos (100+)

# six infant deaths, the same rows in both
#>   IDADE healthbR_age_years md_IDADEanos md_IDADEmeses md_IDADEdias md_IDADEhoras
#> 1   021       3.992699e-05         <NA>          <NA>         <NA>          <NA>
#> 2   101       1.140771e-04         <NA>          <NA>         <NA>             1
#> 3   201       2.737851e-03         <NA>          <NA>            1          <NA>
#> 4   302       1.666667e-01         <NA>             2         <NA>          <NA>
#> 5   102       2.281542e-04         <NA>          <NA>         <NA>             2
#> 6   108       9.126169e-04         <NA>          <NA>         <NA>             8

healthbR (decode_age = TRUE, the default) adds one numeric age_years that is continuous – 21 minutes is 0.00004 years, 2 months is 0.167 – so age bands and rates come out of one column; IDADE itself is kept. microdatasus splits the field into IDADEminutos, IDADEhoras, IDADEdias, IDADEmeses, IDADEanos, each NA outside its unit, which is closer to how the DO form reads and keeps the unit explicit. For adult mortality the two agree to the year; for infant mortality you will reach for different columns.

SINASC: live births, Acre 2022

Measured on 2026-09-05; the offline reproduction re-run on 2026-10-14.

# healthbR
ac_n <- sinasc_data(year = 2022, uf = "AC")
dim(ac_n)
#> [1] 14483    63
class(ac_n$PESO); sum(is.na(ac_n$PESO)); median(ac_n$PESO, na.rm = TRUE)
#> [1] "integer"
#> [1] 94
#> [1] 3230

# microdatasus
ac_nm  <- fetch_datasus(year_start = 2022, year_end = 2022, uf = "AC",
                        information_system = "SINASC")
ac_nmp <- process_sinasc(ac_nm)
sum(is.na(ac_nm$PESO)); sum(is.na(ac_nmp$PESO))
#> [1] 94
#> [1] 14483

Same 14,483 births (3.1 s healthbR; 3.3 s + 3.5 s microdatasus). One thing to know before relying on process_sinasc() in microdatasus 3.0.0: it returns PESO (birth weight) as NA on every row, while the raw column had 94 missing values out of 14,483. The behaviour reproduces offline with the package’s own sample:

library(microdatasus)   # process_sinasc() looks up its tables on the search path
sum(is.na(sinasc_sample$PESO))
#> [1] 2
sum(is.na(process_sinasc(sinasc_sample)$PESO))
#> [1] 100

The recode of the sentinel values ("0" and "9999" to NA) is followed by an as.numeric(), and with dplyr 1.2.1 the whole column comes back missing. It is reported as rfsaldanha/microdatasus#145, still open on 2026-10-14; check the package’s news for your versions, and in the meantime take PESO from the raw tibble. healthbR does not rewrite the column: PESO is parsed to integer and the sentinels are left for you to treat.

Where the bytes come from

healthbR microdatasus read.dbc
SIM, SINASC, SIA, SINAN, CNES DATASUS FTP, .dbc, decompressed locally DATASUS FTP, .dbc, decompressed locally whatever file you downloaded
SIH, SI-PNI healthbr-data mirror: hive-partitioned Parquet on Cloudflare R2, one partition per DATASUS file, byte-identical values, provenance per file; DATASUS FTP as fallback (source = c("r2", "datasus")) DATASUS FTP whatever file you downloaded
Local cache Partitioned Parquet per module (*_cache_status(), *_clear_cache()); a second call never touches the network none (every call downloads) –
Re-issued files sih_status(): MD5 and size per partition, last_updated of the mirror – –
Lazy queries lazy = TRUE, backend = "arrow" or "duckdb", over the cache or the mirror – –
Parallel downloads future::plan(multisession) + furrr sequential –

The mirror is refreshed weekly against the FTP by file size (the FTP offers neither ETag nor hash), and a re-issued file is republished with a new MD5 in the manifest – that is what sih_status() reads.

Other routes

Two other projects answer the same question and were not measured here: PySUS, the Python package that covers SIM, SINASC, SIH, SIA, CNES and SINAN from the same FTP, and basedosdados, which serves treated SIM and SINASC tables through BigQuery with an R client. If your pipeline is in Python, PySUS is the natural pick; if you want SQL over already-treated tables and accept the BigQuery account, basedosdados.

Which one

  • You already have the .dbc files, or want the fewest dependencies: read.dbc, which needs only foreign – installed from the CRAN archive or GitHub since it left CRAN – or microdatasus::read_dbc(), the same job on a CRAN package. read.dbc is also the only one that writes .dbc.
  • You want labels in the tibble and a quick table: microdatasus. process_*() does in one call what would take a few joins in healthbR, and it also brings municipality names and coordinates.
  • You join, compare years, or model: healthbR. Codes stay codes, types are already parsed, dictionaries are functions, and nothing is rewritten under you.
  • You read SIH at scale, or repeatedly: healthbR. Local Parquet cache, lazy arrow/duckdb queries over the mirror, provenance you can cite – or the mirror’s Parquet directly, with arrow or duckdb, if you know the files you want.
  • You need the SIM fetal/infant/maternal extracts, the RJ/SP/ER SIH files, or SIGTAP: microdatasus, which has them and healthbR does not (yet).
  • You need SI-PNI, SISAB, the household surveys, ANS or ANVISA: healthbR; the other two stop at DATASUS.

They also compose. fetch_datasus() and sih_data(parse = FALSE) return the same character columns for the same file, so a script can read with one and label with the other:

# read with healthbR (cache, provenance), label with microdatasus
sih_data(year = 2023, month = 1, uf = "RR", parse = FALSE) |>
  process_sih()

What each package covers

healthbR microdatasus 3.0.0
SIM (mortality) sim_data(): DO, 1996–2024 "SIM-DO", "SIM-DOFET", "SIM-DOEXT", "SIM-DOINF", "SIM-DOMAT"
SINASC (live births) sinasc_data(): 1996–2024 "SINASC"
SIH (admissions) sih_data(): RD (reduced AIH), 1992–2026 "SIH-RD", "SIH-RJ", "SIH-SP", "SIH-ER"
SIA (outpatient) sia_data(): 13 file types, 2008–2026 12 file types
CNES (facilities) cnes_data(): 13 file types, 2005–2026 13 file types
SINAN (notifiable diseases) sinan_data(): 31 diseases, 2007–2026 8 diseases (dengue, chikungunya, zika, malaria, Chagas, visceral and cutaneous leishmaniasis, leptospirosis)
SI-PNI (vaccination) sipni_data(): 1994–2026 –
SISAB (primary care) sisab_data() –
Surveys VIGITEL, PNS, PNAD Continua, POF, Censo denominators –
Regulatory agencies ANS, ANVISA –
Auxiliary tables *_dictionary(), *_variables() per module SIGTAP (fetch_sigtab()), CADGER (fetch_cadger()), tabMun, tabCBO, tabOcupacao, tabNaturalidade

read.dbc has no catalogue: it reads any .dbc you point it at, from any system, including the ones neither package wraps. microdatasus goes deeper into SIM and SIH (the fetal, external-cause, infant and maternal SIM extracts; the RJ, SP and ER SIH files) and ships the SIGTAP procedure table. healthbR goes wider: more SINAN diseases, SI-PNI, SISAB, the household surveys and the regulatory agencies, all under one *_years() / *_data() / *_dictionary() API.

Reproducing this vignette

The two SIH files are 349 KB and 16.4 MB. To rerun the comparison:

install.packages(c("microdatasus", "arrow", "duckdb", "bench"))
install.packages(
  "https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/read.dbc/read.dbc_1.2.0.tar.gz",
  repos = NULL, type = "source"
)
# install.packages("pak"); pak::pak("SidneyBissoli/healthbR")   # dev version

# a cold healthbR run: a new R session and an empty cache directory
d <- tempfile(); dir.create(d)
system.time(sih_data(year = 2023, month = 1, uf = "SP", cache_dir = d))
system.time(fetch_datasus(2023, 1, 2023, 1, uf = "SP",
                          information_system = "SIH-RD"))
